summary: Many Internet applications fetch resources available on several equivalent hosts, including peer-to-peer file sharing. Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) aims to give guidance about which hosts to choose. This informational document discusses practical considerations for deploying ALTO.

plainLanguage.summary: If many shops sell the same toy, a guide can tell you which is closest. This talks about how to set up that guide so programs can pick better places to download from.

subtitle: Practical guidance for deploying ALTO to optimize application performance across networks.

tldr.problem: Applications that fetch resources from multiple servers have no way to know which servers are closer or cheaper to reach, leading to poor performance and network waste.
tldr.mechanism: ALTO is a client-server protocol where applications query an ALTO server for guidance about which resource providers to prefer based on network topology and costs.
tldr.outcome: This informational document guides network operators and application designers on how to deploy ALTO for peer-to-peer file sharing, content delivery networks, and other applications.

facts.label: Two main ALTO services
facts.value: Network/Cost Maps and Endpoint Cost Service

facts.label: Primary use cases
facts.value: Peer-to-peer file sharing and content delivery networks

today: RFC 7971 is an Informational document providing deployment guidance for ALTO. ALTO has been deployed by some ISPs and content delivery networks, though widespread adoption has been limited. The protocol remains a viable way for networks to expose topology information to applications, particularly for peer-to-peer and CDN services.

sections.title: What ALTO Does
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) helps applications choose better servers. When an application can fetch a file from multiple hosts, it queries an ALTO server to learn which hosts are closest, cheapest, or least congested. This lets the application and the network both benefit: the application gets faster downloads while the network avoids expensive inter-domain traffic.

This RFC discusses practical deployment issues. It covers use cases like peer-to-peer file sharing and content delivery networks, shows how to generate ALTO information, and provides recommendations for network operators and application designers. The ALTO protocol itself is defined in RFC 7285, and the problem space is described in RFC 5693.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO tells programs which server to pick. This document is about how to build and use ALTO in real networks with real operators and applications.

sections.title: ALTO Entities and Deployment Models
sections.content:
ALTO has four key roles: a source of topological information, an ALTO server, ALTO clients, and resource consumers. A resource consumer is the application endpoint that wants to download a file. The ALTO client is the software library that queries the server. These roles can be separated: the ALTO server may be run by the ISP while clients are embedded in applications, or clients may run on a resource directory like a BitTorrent tracker.

There are two main deployment patterns: clients embedded in endpoints make direct queries to the ALTO server, or clients embedded in a resource directory make queries once and return guidance to many endpoints. Both patterns are valid depending on the application architecture. The ALTO server itself is a logical entity that can be implemented by multiple physical servers using load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO has four moving parts: the source of network knowledge, the ALTO server that answers questions, the client code in applications, and the user code that wants a file. These can be split between endpoints and directories.

sections.title: Gathering and Provisioning Network Information
sections.content:
To provide useful guidance, an ALTO server must gather topology data from many sources: routing protocols, network policies, performance measurements, geolocation, and more. The server then aggregates this data into abstract maps that group IP addresses into network locations and assign costs between them. The RFC discusses data sources, methods for aggregating and partitioning IP ranges, cost calculation approaches, and monitoring techniques.

A critical design choice is how much detail to expose. The ALTO protocol supports two modes: Network and Cost Maps that expose pre-computed costs between regions (the client does not reveal which servers it is considering), and Endpoint Cost Services where the client lists candidate servers and the server ranks them (the server learns about the client's options). Each approach has different privacy implications and operational complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The ALTO server gathers network knowledge from routing, measurements, and policies. It then creates maps grouping addresses and assigning costs between them. Different maps reveal different amounts of detail about the network.

sections.title: Using ALTO for Peer-to-Peer Applications
sections.content:
In peer-to-peer file sharing, ALTO helps peers find other peers with the file. A peer queries ALTO to learn which candidate peers are in the same ISP network (cheap to reach) or at least in the same region (cheaper to reach remotely). This is valuable because peer networks often have thousands of candidates and most of the cost is inter-domain traffic.

The RFC notes that ALTO clients in peer applications can run either at each peer (if every peer makes queries) or at the tracker (if the tracker queries once and sends rankings to all peers asking for the file). The tracker approach is more efficient: it reduces load on the ALTO server and requires fewer queries. However, some peer applications run without a tracker, in which case each peer must have an ALTO client.
sections.plainLanguage: When a peer-to-peer program wants a file, ALTO tells it which other peers are closest. It can do this at the peer itself or at a central tracker. Using a tracker is cheaper and faster.

sections.title: Using ALTO for Content Delivery Networks
sections.content:
Content delivery networks (CDNs) serve popular content from servers near users. A CDN can use ALTO to learn where a client is located in the network, then direct the client to the nearest CDN server. ALTO is valuable here because it gives the CDN knowledge of network topology without having to perform active measurements for every client.

CDN deployments of ALTO typically use the Endpoint Cost Service: the CDN tells ALTO "here is a client IP, rank my servers by cost to that client." This lets CDNs provide localized responses without building their own comprehensive network maps. The RFC discusses deployment considerations including which ALTO services to use and how to handle scenarios where the client is not in the ALTO server's database.
sections.plainLanguage: A content delivery network uses ALTO to find the nearest server for each user. ALTO tells it which of its servers is closest to the user's location in the network.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Issues
sections.content:
ALTO crosses trust boundaries: an application in one network queries a server run by another. Network operators worry about leaking topology information that could reveal bottlenecks or be used for attacks. The RFC addresses concerns about the ALTO server revealing too much detail, the integrity of ALTO responses, and access control (who is allowed to query the server).

The RFC recommends that ALTO servers abstract their topology appropriately for their threat model, that ALTO be combined with authentication and authorization if needed, and that operators monitor the impact of ALTO traffic on their networks. It also notes that applications must work even if ALTO is unavailable or unresponsive.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators are careful about sharing topology information. ALTO must not leak secrets about how the network is built. Access must be controlled and monitored.

left.title: Endpoint clients
left.desc: Each endpoint's ALTO client queries the server directly.

right.title: Directory client
right.desc: A central tracker queries once and guides all endpoints.
